methodology: AssemblyAI Universal-2-TF (arXiv:2501.05948): `target` is text that already has correct punctuation and casing; `input` is the same text lowercased and stripped of punctuation, simulating raw ASR output. Score = how well the formatter restores `target` from `input`.

librispeech-pc.name: LibriSpeech-PC
librispeech-pc.license_evidence: LICENSE.txt inside manifests.tar.gz itself: 'The LibriSpeech-PC Dataset is made available by NVIDIA CORPORATION under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.'
librispeech-pc.citation: A. Meister, M. Novikov, N. Karpov, E. Bakhturina, V. Lavrukhin, B. Ginsburg, "LibriSpeech-PC: Benchmark for Evaluation of Punctuation and Capitalization Capabilities of end-to-end ASR Models," arXiv:2310.02943, 2023.
librispeech-pc.caveat: READ speech: LibriVox volunteers reading pre-1928 Gutenberg prose, via the original LibriSpeech corpus. Zero fillers, and a comma distribution drawn from long literary sentences. It measures punctuation/casing restoration and NOTHING about disfluency -- optimizing the formatter against this corpus alone could actively harm real dictation output. Treat it as a regression guard, not a target.

earnings22.name: Earnings-22
earnings22.license_evidence: earnings22/LICENSE.md in the repo: 'The transcripts and associated text files that are used for alignment in this directory are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.'
earnings22.citation: M. Del Rio et al., "Earnings-22: A Practical Benchmark for Accents in Speech Recognition," Research in Language 21(3), 2023 (arXiv:2203.15591).
earnings22.caveat: Spontaneous speech (earnings calls), real fillers ('um'/'uh' appear as ordinary tokens on BOTH sides here). This entry covers the full 125-call corpus, whose transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp are verbatim, token-level, punctuation+case-tagged references -- one transcript per call, so on its own it supports kind=punctuation only. The verbatim/non-verbatim PAIR a disfluency fixture needs does exist, for ten of these calls, under earnings22/subset10/ -- see the separate `earnings22-subset10` source, which is where every kind=disfluency case from Earnings-22 comes from. None of the ten subset10 calls appears in the sample here -- asserted in the fetch script -- so the punctuation and disfluency fixtures share no audio and no transcript text.

earnings22-subset10.name: Earnings-22 Subset 10
earnings22-subset10.license_evidence: earnings22/subset10/LICENSE.md, the subset's OWN license file (not inherited from the parent directory): 'The transcripts and associated text files that are used for alignment in this directory are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.'
earnings22-subset10.citation: Q. McNamara, M. A. del Rio Fernandez, N. Bhandari, M. Ratajczak, D. Chen, C. Miller, M. Jette, "Style-agnostic evaluation of ASR using multiple reference transcripts," arXiv:2412.07937, 2024 -- the paper describing this subset's creation; the underlying calls are Earnings-22 (Del Rio et al., Research in Language 21(3), 2023).
earnings22-subset10.caveat: THE VERBATIM/NON-VERBATIM PAIR. Ten Earnings-22 calls were re-transcribed in a second style and shipped under earnings22/subset10/. Its README states the difference first-hand: 'The verbatim transcripts are created by the transcriptionists writing exactly what they hear, including filler words, stutters, interjections (active listening) and repetitions. The nonverbatim transcripts are created by lightly editing for readability without changing the structure or meaning of the speech.' Why it is easy to miss: subset10/verbatim_transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp are git SYMLINKS (mode 120000) back to ../../../transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp, so the verbatim half looks identical to the full corpus and only subset10/nonverbatim_transcripts/ is new. Looking only at earnings22/transcripts/ therefore shows one transcript per call and nothing else, which is the wrong conclusion. HOW THE CASES ARE DERIVED, since upstream ships no sentence-level alignment: the two token streams are aligned with difflib, cut into units only where BOTH sides end a sentence at the same aligned token, and a unit is kept only if it is DELETION-ONLY -- the non-verbatim side is the verbatim side with whole tokens deleted and, on each token that survives, punctuation characters deleted; nothing inserted, nothing substituted, nothing re-cased, punctuation included -- AND every deleted run is a recognisable disfluency: a filler ('uh', 'um', ...), an immediate repetition of a word that SURVIVES next to it, or a false start (Rev marks these with a trailing hyphen, e.g. 'curren-'). Punctuation may vanish because that is a mechanical consequence of the deletion -- the commas in 'So, obviously higher margins, uh, excluding those sales.' exist only to set off the filler -- but punctuation that is ADDED ('So' -> 'So,'), SWAPPED ('detail.' -> 'detail?') or used to merge two sentences into one ('CapEx. Um, our guidance' -> 'CapEx, our guidance') is a rewrite and the unit is discarded, as it is where the transcriptionist also reworded ('gonna' -> 'going to'), corrected a mishearing, dropped an ordinary word, or restyled capitalisation. Those are editorial choices a formatter cannot be expected to reproduce, and scoring them would put an unreachable ceiling on the metric. 260 of 4566 candidate units survive (5.7%); the script prints this on every run. WHAT THIS FIXTURE THEREFORE DOES NOT MEASURE, which is a consequence of the filter's construction and not a sampling accident: SELF-CORRECTIONS ('we grew three, sorry, four percent') and RESTARTS that are not hyphen-marked are absent by design. A correction replaces one word with a different one, so the aligner sees a `replace` and the unit is discarded; an abandoned phrase that Rev did not mark with a trailing hyphen is an unexplained deletion and is discarded too. The tag counts on the committed sample show the shape of what is left: filler 152, repetition 79, false-start 13 out of 200 cases. So this fixture measures REMOVAL OF FILLERS AND REPETITIONS well, false starts thinly, and self-corrections not at all -- and it does not measure the full verbatim-to-readable rewrite Rev's transcriptionists actually performed. Disfl-QA is the complement here: over 90% of ITS disfluencies are corrections and restarts, but it is written text rather than speech.

disflqa.name: Disfl-QA
disflqa.license_evidence: README.md, '## License' section: 'Disfl-QA dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.'
disflqa.citation: A. Gupta, J. Xu, S. Upadhyay, D. Yang, M. Faruqui, "Disfl-QA: A Benchmark Dataset for Understanding Disfluencies in Question Answering," Findings of ACL, 2021.
disflqa.caveat: ~12k (disfluent, original) question pairs built on SQuAD-v2; over 90% of disfluencies are corrections or restarts. Written text, not ASR transcripts -- both sides start already cased and punctuated, so `verbatim` here carries the disfluent question in its original casing/punctuation and `input` is `tools/fetch_corpora.py`'s lowercase/unpunctuated simulation of it.

indic-diarbench.name: Indic DiarBench (sarvamai/indic-diarbench)
indic-diarbench.license_evidence: Hugging Face dataset card metadata, machine-readable: cardData.license == "cc-by-4.0" (confirmed via https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/sarvamai/indic-diarbench).
indic-diarbench.citation: Sarvam AI, "Indic DiarBench: A Multilingual Joint Diarization and ASR Benchmark for Indian Languages," Interspeech 2026 (arXiv:2607.23808).
indic-diarbench.caveat: REGIONAL-LANGUAGE REGRESSION GUARD, NOT A QUALITY TARGET -- this project's stated priority is English formatting first. Natural multi-speaker conversational Hindi with real Devanagari danda punctuation, published by this app's own ASR vendor. Scoped to the Hindi config only, out of the 22 languages the full benchmark covers, and audio is never downloaded, only the `annotated_transcript` text. Segments that are pure non-speech tags (<noise>, <unintelligible>, <background_speech>) are dropped rather than treated as text. MEASURED ANNOTATION ARTIFACT, do not read a score here without it: this benchmark glosses code-mixed and spelled-out words by appending the Latin-script or numeric form in parentheses -- 'एग्जेग्टली(exactly)', 'तीस(30)'. Counted over the committed sample, 69.5% of cases contain at least one such gloss and parentheses are 956 of the 1432 restorable punctuation marks (67%) -- so a majority of the punctuation 'restoration' being scored is really reinstating a transcription convention, not a formatting behaviour any dictation user wants (no formatter can derive '(30)' from the spelled-out word). Those cases are TAGGED rather than dropped, because dropping them would shrink an intentional regression guard: `english-gloss` marks a case containing any such gloss, and `gloss-dominated` marks the subset where parentheses are at least half that case's punctuation. A report should separate them, and should not present the gloss-dominated subset as a formatting-quality number.
